name: carbonx_ask_dna
description: Ask Carbon-X a question about DNA sequences you supply. It is a 14.8B language model trained jointly on DNA and English: give it named sequences and a question and it answers in prose, with its reasoning. It is strongest on variant effects (is this change benign or pathogenic), sequence features (enhancer vs promoter, organism group, motifs, transcription-factor binding sites) and next-base prediction. It is WEAK on splice sites and histone marks, it miscounts bases and coordinates, and it was not trained to design sequences. The answer is a model prediction, NOT clinically validated, and must not drive a medical decision. Sequences are DNA only; 'sequences' is required, because this tool answers questions about DNA rather than acting as a general assistant. The prompt is limited to about 7,168 tokens (roughly 43 kbp of DNA); a longer one is refused by name with its real token count.

question.description: What to ask about the sequences. Put everything in one question: Carbon-X was trained and evaluated with the sequence and the question in a single message. For a variant, give the position and the reference and alternate base, computed in code rather than left to the model to locate.

sequences.description: The DNA to ask about, as name -> sequence. Names are how the question refers to them ('reference', 'variant', 'promoter'). IUPAC ambiguity codes are accepted but cost resolution: only A, C, G and T form 6-mer tokens, and any 6-mer containing another character collapses into one <oov> token. At most {...} sequences.

context.description: What is already known: gene, strand, assembly, coordinates, annotations. Placed before the question. Upstream's strongest prompting advice -- without it the model may invent a sequence's identity or function.

max_tokens.description: Ceiling on the answer, 1 to {...}. Generation measured about 12-14 tokens per second on the verified card, so this is the main thing that sets how long a call takes. The reply says whether the answer was truncated.

seed.description: Random seed. Carbon-X's published results use sampling (temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, top-k 20), so answers vary; pass a seed to repeat one.

test_examples.question: Is this sequence more likely coding or non-coding? Answer in one or two sentences.
test_examples.context: Human HBB (beta-globin), the first 55 bases of the coding sequence on the plus strand.
